html:
The sale in 1803 by France to the United States of its claim to Louisiana, the huge basin west of the Mississippi River. For about fifteen million dollars the United States roughly doubled in size.

France had handed Louisiana to Spain in 1762 (Spanish Louisiana) and got it back in secret in 1800. President Thomas Jefferson only wanted New Orleans, the port that farmers on the western rivers depended on. But Napoleon had just lost an army trying to retake Saint-Domingue, where the Haitian Revolution had freed the enslaved, and he expected war with Britain. Without Haiti, Louisiana was of little use to him, and he offered the whole territory.

What was sold was a European claim, not empty land. The lands of the Osage, Quapaw, Lakota, Pawnee and many other nations were never asked about. The United States later took them by treaties, purchases and wars. Old French and Spanish posts such as Natchitoches came under American rule.

Jefferson sent Lewis and Clark up the Missouri River in 1804 to explore the new land and reach the Pacific. In time the purchase gave the land for all or part of fifteen states, and the question of whether slavery would spread into it helped drive the country toward civil war.
